lines.cap: **Narrator:** Four p.m. Room 8H. Outside, Singapore's daily monsoon has arrived right on schedule.
**Narrator:** Mr Hargreaves has reached mug twenty-one. Mei has written one sentence.
**Mei:** 'It was a **dark and stormy** night, and the hawker centre was **very, very** busy and nice!!!'
**Nib:** Three exclamation marks and Edward Bulwer-Lytton's **1830** cliché! I have leaked through the desk!
**Addie:** Addie! Adjective enthusiast! Needs more adjectives! Make it a **big, loud, hot, crowded, amazing** hawker centre!
**Cam:** Cut, cut, CUT! Cam. Cinema zoom lens. I can't film 'busy' or 'nice'! What am I actually **looking** at?!
**Will:** In **1599** I wrecked an entire ship on a bare wooden stage using nothing but **words**. Today Mei gives description **one star**.
**Mei:** Because nothing **happens** in a description! You just stare at a picture!
**Mr H:** Put the exclamation marks down, 8H. Let's step into the rain.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode fourteen: It Was a Dark and Stormy Period Three.

chapters.title: Show, don't tell — and use all five senses

lines.cap: **Narrator:** The hawker centre at dusk. Cam is framing the shot.
**Mr H:** **Telling** names a quality or feeling directly: 'The hawker centre was busy. Mei was nervous.'
**Cam:** **Showing** gives the camera and microphone **evidence** so the reader infers the feeling themselves!
**Mei:** Like: 'Every plastic stool was taken, and the chicken-rice queue coiled past the drinks stall'?
**Mr H:** Spot on. Don't write 'the old man was poor'. Write: 'he counted his coins twice, then put the smallest one back.'
**Nib:** Once you've **shown** the evidence, one short plain statement afterwards — 'It was the loudest place on earth' — lands hard.
**Cam:** Now switch on **all five senses**! Remember: **S**ome **H**ungry **S**harks **T**aste **T**oes — Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, Touch.
**Mei:** Got it! 'I could see smoke. I could hear a wok. I could smell garlic—'
**Nib:** Stop! '**I could see, I could hear**' turns your paragraph into a shopping list and shoves **you** in the way!
**Mr H:** Cut 'I could hear' and let **onomatopoeia** strike directly: the bright **clang** of the wok; bean sprouts **hissing** in hot oil.
**Will:** **Smell** goes straight to memory: charcoal smoke, wet earth after rain, kaya toast at dawn.
**Nib:** And for top marks, try **synaesthesia** — blending two senses: jasmine so fragrant '**the air tastes sweet**'.
**Addie:** Ooh, metaphor time! 'The rain fell like cats and dogs, and the MRT was as **cold as ice**!'
**Nib:** **Clichés**, darling! Dead comparisons examiners have read ten thousand times! Reject your first idea.
**Mr H:** Climb the **cliché ladder** using the world of your scene: not 'cold as ice', but '**cold as the MRT air-con at seven a.m.**'
**Mei:** And tropical rain isn't 'cats and dogs' — it falls in '**straight silver rods**', or dusk turns the colour of **teh tarik**!
**Cam:** Use **personification**: 'At Raffles Place the doors **sighed** open, and the carriage **breathed out** a crowd.'
**Nib:** When weather or setting mirrors human emotion, call it **pathetic fallacy** — coined by **John Ruskin** in **1856**.
**Mei:** Wait — doesn't 'pathetic' mean sad and useless?
**Nib:** Greek **pathos**, meaning **feeling**! Sunshine at a joyful wedding is pathetic fallacy too, not only storms.
**Will:** Hear Miranda's storm in **The Tempest**: 'the sea, mounting to th' welkin's cheek, / Dashes the fire out.'
**Mr H:** One warning: don't cram five similes into one sentence. **Purple prose** Tangled in mixed metaphors blurs the picture.
**Mei:** Two stars. Mainly because 'the carriage breathed out a crowd' is painfully accurate.

chapters.title: Sack the adjectives, hire a verb

lines.cap: **Addie:** Look at my masterpiece! 'The **very big, dark, old, scary, creepy** shophouse!' Five adjectives! Beat that!
**Mr H:** That's an **adjective pile**, Addie. Each vague adjective dilutes the last, and most of them are tells.
**Nib:** In strong description, **precise nouns** and **vivid verbs** do the heavy lifting.
**Mei:** So not 'a bird in a tree eating food' — a **mynah** in a **rain tree** eyeing my **char kway teow**!
**Mr H:** And cut weak **verb plus adverb**. Don't write 'the jogger **ran quickly**'. Use one verb: '**sprinted**' or '**pounded**'.
**Cam:** Watch how one verb changes the whole character: he **trudged**, he **stormed**, he **slunk** down the road.
**Will:** Lord Tennyson needed one verb for an ocean seen from a cliff: '**The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls.**'
**Mei:** '**Crawls**'! That makes the giant sea look tiny, slow and insect-like from the eagle's height!
**Nib:** Check **connotations** too: **slim**, **skinny** and **scrawny** all denote thin, yet move from admiring to frail.
**Addie:** Fine! I bought a thesaurus! 'The **effulgent** sun irradiated the **crepuscular** firmament!'
**Mr H:** The **thesaurus trap**. Never swallow a dictionary to sound clever; pick words the reader can **picture**.

chapters.title: Move the camera — don't start a car chase

lines.cap: **Mei:** Paragraph two! Suddenly ninjas rob the drink stall, Uncle Lim jumps a motorbike, and—
**Cam:** FREEZE FRAME! That's a **story**, Mei! In a description, the **place and atmosphere** are the star!
**Cam:** Structure your piece by **moving the camera**: start with a wide **drone shot**, then zoom in step by step.
**Mr H:** Paragraph one, **background**: from the bus, the hawker roof glows amber like a **lantern** among dark HDB blocks.
**Cam:** Paragraph two, **midground**: inside the heat, ceiling fans churning, the char kway teow uncle inside a cloud of smoke.
**Cam:** Paragraph three, **close-up detail**: table thirty-four — a grandmother's patient fingers peeling prawns beside a **packet of tissues**.
**Mr H:** Paragraph four: a **shift in mood or weather**, signalled by a **one-line paragraph**: '**Then the sky split open.**'
**Nib:** End with a **cyclical structure**: return to the opening **lantern** roof from the bus stop — still glowing in the rain.
**Kevin:** Start a new paragraph with **TiPToP**: change of **Time, Place, Topic or Person**!
**Mr H:** And pick **one tense** and **one viewpoint**. 'The rain **hammers** the roof; a cyclist **skidded**' breaks the spell.
**Mr H:** Listen to your rhythm. If every sentence is twelve words starting with 'The', your paragraph flatlines.
**Cam:** Build a **city skyline**: long flowing sentences for panorama, then a sudden **short sentence** for impact!
**Nib:** Five shapes — **S**ome **L**azy **C**ats **F**ear **M**ice: **Short**, **List**, **Complex**, **Fronted adverbial**, and **Minor sentence**.
**Will:** Dickens opens **Bleak House** with a two-word minor sentence: '**Fog everywhere.**' No main verb — the fog simply sits there.
**Nib:** Punctuation controls **timing**. A **colon** holds your breath before a reveal: 'There was only one sound**:** the drip of the tap.'
**Mr H:** A **semicolon** balances two linked sentences; a **dash** jolts: 'The sea was calm **—** too calm.'
**Kevin:** Never stick me between two full sentences! 'The rain stopped, the steam rose' is a **comma splice**! Put me after a **fronted adverbial**: 'Beneath the awning, steam rose!'
**Mr H:** Finally, plan your picture in **three layers** — background, midground, foreground — and redraft with **ARMS**.
**Mei:** **Remove** & **Substitute**: cut 'very busy and nice'; swap 'ran quickly' for 'sprinted' and 'food' for 'char kway teow'.
**Mei:** **Add** & **Move**: add charcoal smoke and a short minor sentence — 'Nobody spoke.' — saving the strongest image for last!
**Addie:** Okay... one single precise verb **did** look cooler than five 'verys'. Don't tell anyone.
**Narrator:** The rain eases. Room 8H packs its descriptive toolkit.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! Senses: **Some Hungry Sharks Taste Toes**. Sentences: **Some Lazy Cats Fear Mice**. Paragraphs: **TiPToP**. Redrafting: **ARMS**!
**Cam:** One. Don't turn a description into an action **story**! Move the camera — wide shot to close-up to cyclical echo.
**Addie:** Two. Ditch **adjective piles** and 'very'. Let **specific nouns** and **vivid verbs** do the work.
**Nib:** Three. Ban the mechanical checklist '**I could see, I could hear**', and swap dead **clichés** for fresh local images.
**Mr H:** Four. Never drift between **past and present tense** without a deliberate reason.
**Kevin:** Five. No **comma splices** and no triple exclamation marks! Use a colon, semicolon and dash deliberately.
**Will:** Six. Avoid the **thesaurus trap** and five-simile purple prose. Control beats showing off.
**Mei:** Descriptive Writing: **four stars**. I can actually smell the char kway teow now.
**Will:** Four stars?! After Miranda's tempest?!
**Mei:** My shoes got soaked during location filming.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** What is the difference between **telling** and **showing**?
**Mei:** **Telling** names a feeling directly; **showing** gives sensory details and actions so the reader infers it.
**Mr H:** When stormy weather mirrors a character's inner turmoil, what is that technique called?
**Nib:** **Pathetic fallacy** — from the Greek **pathos**, meaning feeling.
**Mr H:** Why is 'The eagle watched as the wrinkled sea **crawls**' better than piling up five adjectives?
**Will:** One **precise verb** carries movement, scale and mood without clutter.
**Mr H:** What is a **minor sentence**, and why must you use it sparingly?
**Cam:** A deliberate fragment with **no main verb**, like '**Fog everywhere.**' Rare ones create impact; too many lose force.
**Mr H:** What do the four letters of **ARMS** stand for when redrafting?
**Kevin:** **Add**, **Remove**, **Move**, **Substitute**!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Descriptive Writing** quiz in your English Lab.
**Addie:** Can I keep just **one** tiny 'very'?
**Nib:** No.
